Now let me fetch a few more specific sources for denominational views:Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 36, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## Ezekiel 36 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview / Structure

The chapter falls into two main sections: (1) God's promise to restore the land of Israel (vv. 1–15), and (2) God's promise to spiritually renew the people of Israel (vv. 16–38). The pivot between them is God's concern for His own holy name.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

Ezekiel 36 parallels the New Covenant promises of Jeremiah 31, including three elements: (a) restoration to the land (v. 24), (b) forgiveness of sin (v. 25), and (c) the indwelling Holy Spirit (vv. 26–27).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-36.html (Dr. Constable)

---

### v. 1 — "Prophesy to the mountains of Israel…"

**Traditional reading:** The "mountains of Israel" stand by personification for the land and the people. In Ezekiel 6:1–3 the mountains were addressed in denunciation because of idolatry upon them; now they are addressed in consolation. Though the people are in exile, the land itself remains and God has enduring interest in the literal territory.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary (F. F. Bruce)
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html (Ellicott)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

Matthew Henry notes that since the people were gone, nothing remained to be spoken to except the mountains and valleys — "these the Chaldeans could not carry away with them."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary

---

### v. 2 — "The ancient heights have become our possession"

**Traditional reading:** The "enemy" (a general term for surrounding nations, especially Edom) gloated that the "everlasting hills" (cf. Gen 49:26; Deut 33:15) were now theirs. By boasting "Aha!" they expressed malicious joy over Judah's defeat. The phrase is probably an allusion to the patriarchal promises — the nations were claiming that God's promise to His people had failed.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary

---

### v. 3 — "Made you desolate … trampled you on every side"

**Traditional reading:** The verb translated "swallowed you up" (or "trampled") literally means "to pant or snuff up," a figure from the panting of wild beasts ravenously smelling after prey. The land became "a by-word and a reproach" (cf. Deut 28:37; 1 Kings 9:7). The phrase "taken up in slander by the lips of their talkers" (or "the gossip and slander of the people" — NET) indicates Israel had become the subject of derisive whispering among the nations.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Feinberg and Block)
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary

---

### v. 4 — "O mountains and hills … ravines and valleys … desolate ruins and abandoned cities"

**Traditional reading:** The address broadens from mountains to every feature of the devastated landscape. The text is "tremulous with emotion" (Peake). God sees and names every aspect of the land's ruin — the topography, the desolate wastes, the forsaken cities — showing His intimate concern for the land itself. The land had become "a spoil and a mockery to the rest of the nations."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-36.html (Peake)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

---

### v. 5 — "In My burning zeal … against all Edom"

**Traditional reading:** God's "burning jealousy" (or "burning zeal") is His holy resentment against indignities done to Himself and His land. Edom is singled out because they took Israel's land "with wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (literally "with spiteful minds"). The land is explicitly called "My land" — it belongs to Yahweh even when Israel is exiled (cf. Lev 25:23, "the land is Mine"). Trapp comments: "Jealousy is hot as hell; it is implacable, and very vindictive."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html (Expositor's Bible)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Trapp)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary

---

### v. 6 — "Because you have endured the reproach of the nations"

**Traditional reading:** God's zeal is aroused not by Israel's merit but by the shame the land has borne. Block comments: "The land has borne the insults of the nations long enough, and Yahweh's own passion has been ignited. He will have the last word."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

---

### v. 7 — "I have sworn with an uplifted hand"

**Traditional reading:** The uplifted hand is an oath gesture (cf. Ezek 20:6). God solemnly swears that the nations who shamed Israel will themselves bear their own shame. Poole says Moabites, Ammonites, and Edomites "shall be repaid in their own coin."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Poole)

---

### v. 8 — "You will produce branches and bear fruit for My people Israel, for they will soon come home"

**Traditional reading:** The land is now promised to "shoot forth" its branches and yield fruit. The return of the people is described as imminent ("soon come home" / "about to come"). Ellicott calls this "a strong and vivid way of setting forth at once the certainty and the nearness of the return."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

**Dispensational/Literalist note:** Precept Austin (citing Gaebelein, MacArthur, Walvoord) insists this prophecy "can only be fulfilled in future millennial blessing to Israel that she has not yet experienced." The return from Babylon was only a partial fulfillment; the full fulfillment awaits the millennial kingdom.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary

---

### vv. 9–10 — "I am on your side … you will be tilled and sown … I will multiply the people upon you"

**Traditional reading:** Block notes a "clever and unique wordplay" — the usual hostile "I am against you" (hineni alekem) is transformed into "I am on your side" ("I am for you"). The promise is for the entire house of Israel ("all of it"). Cities inhabited, ruins rebuilt.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

F. B. Meyer offers a spiritual application: "Do you think that you will never be glad again… It shall not be so. O desolate mountains, ye shall shoot forth your branches, and yield fruit; and it is near to come."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

---

### v. 11 — "I will make you prosper more than before"

**Traditional reading:** God promises not just restoration but improvement over Israel's former state — "better for you than at your beginnings." The language "multiply and be fruitful" echoes the creation blessing of Genesis 1:22, 28. Block notes the echo of the divine blessing formula.

**Ellicott's caveat:** The language "goes far beyond the historic fulfilment" if taken only literally, and therefore "these earthly blessings are the shadow and type by which is set forth the higher spiritual blessing given to the Church without stint." The "better than at your beginnings" can only be "considered as fulfilled in the spiritual blessings … of the Messianic kingdom."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

---

### v. 12 — "You will no longer deprive them of their children"

**Traditional reading:** In the worst days, the land seemed to work against its inhabitants — through war, famine, and pestilence — "bereaving" them of their children. God promises this curse will be reversed: the land will be a blessing, not a threat.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

---

### vv. 13–15 — "You devour men …"

**Traditional reading:** The land's bad reputation echoed the unfaithful spies' report in Numbers 13:32 ("a land that devours its inhabitants"). Due to droughts (Jer 14:1), blasting and mildew (Amos 4:9), locusts (Joel 1), and famine (Hag 1:10–11), the land had acquired an "unenviable reputation for barrenness" among the nations (The Expositor's Bible). God promises that the land will no longer devour men, the taunts of the nations will cease, and the land will no longer cause the nation to stumble.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Feinberg)

**Modern fulfillment note:** Enduring Word (Guzik) cites modern Israeli agricultural statistics — tripling of farmland and sixteenfold increase in production since 1948 — as "a mere beginning of the much greater fruitfulness promised in the fullness of God's plan."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

**Ellicott's important historical caveat:** Since Edom has long since disappeared as a nation, "whatever is to be literally understood in the prophecy must have been long ago fulfilled." The blessings "were fulfilled literally as far as the sinfulness of the people allowed," but because the people's sin prevented full realization, and since "no future realisation of these is possible, on account of the total change of conditions and circumstances, it is plain that under these earthly terms the prophet … sets forth the glories of the spiritual future."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

---

### vv. 16–19 — Israel's past defilement and judgment

**Traditional reading:** This begins a separate (but connected) prophecy. Israel defiled the land by bloodshed (possibly murders, judicial violence, and child sacrifice — Feinberg) and by idols. Their behavior before God was "like the uncleanness of a woman's impurity" (a Levitical comparison from Lev 15:19). Therefore God poured out His wrath, scattering them among the nations, judging them "according to their ways and deeds." The Exile was necessary for vindicating God's holiness as reflected in the sanctity of His land.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Feinberg)

---

### vv. 20–21 — "They profaned My holy name … I had concern for My holy name"

**Traditional reading:** The Israelites profaned God's name among the nations not only by their sinful conduct (cf. Rom 2:24) but by the very fact of their exile. The nations, thinking of Yahweh as merely a tribal deity, concluded He was too weak to protect His people: "These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land." Thus God's reputation was compromised. But God "had concern" (or "had pity") for His holy name — His own honour was at stake.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Alexander, Taylor, Block)

---

### vv. 22–23 — "Not for your sake … but for My holy name"

**Traditional reading:** This is the theological heart of the chapter. God acts not because Israel deserves it but to vindicate His own name. Ellicott calls this "the constant burden of God's teaching to His people throughout their history" (cf. Exod 32; Num 14; Deut 9). God will "show the holiness of My great name" — sanctifying Himself in the eyes of the nations by restoring Israel. The nations will know that He is the LORD "when I show My holiness in you before their eyes."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

The Expositor's Bible adds: "God cannot disown His ancient people, for that would be to stultify the whole past revelation of His character … therefore Jehovah must carry through His purpose by sanctifying Himself in the salvation of Israel."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

**Reformed emphasis:** God's motivation in salvation is ultimately His own glory, not human worthiness. This verse is foundational for the Reformed doctrine that salvation is *soli Deo gloria* — for God's glory alone. Michael Barrett (Monergism) writes that God's grace is "efficacious" — it accomplishes what it intends, rooted in God's own purpose, not human merit.
— https://www.monergism.com/efficacious-grace-%E2%80%93-ezekiel-3622%E2%80%9332 (seen in search excerpt)

---

### v. 24 — "I will take you from among the nations and gather you … bring you back into your own land"

**Traditional reading:** The gathering from "all countries" points beyond the Babylonian return to a greater regathering (Clarke: "This does not relate to the restoration from Babylon merely. The Jews are at this day scattered in all … countries. From these they are to be gathered"). This is a common feature of new covenant promises (cf. Deut 30:1–6; Jer 23:3; Jer 32:37; Ezek 11:16–17).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Clarke, Wiersbe)

---

### v. 25 — "I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean"

**Traditional reading:** The imagery is drawn from Levitical ritual washings (water mingled with the ashes of a red heifer for purification from corpse-defilement — Num 19; also Lev 14:5–7; Exod 30:17–21). The "truth symbolised is the forgiveness of sins, the act of grace which takes away the effect of moral uncleanness as a barrier to fellowship with God" (Expositor's Bible).

Ellicott adds that Ezekiel "speaks primarily of the cleansing from idolatry and such gross outward sins, and he treats of the people collectively; yet this purification, as the following verses show, must necessarily extend much farther, and be applied to them individually."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

**Connection to baptism:** Ellicott explicitly links this to baptism: "It was the same symbolism which led in later ages to the use of baptism in the admission of proselytes to the Jewish Church … Baptism is also alluded to by our Lord Himself in His conversation with Nicodemus (John 3:5) and afterwards established by Him as the initiatory sacrament of the Christian Church." Enduring Word similarly says this "is the likely connection Jesus had in mind when He spoke of being born of water in John 3:5."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

**Lutheran note:** From the search excerpt, Ligonier's Reformed study notes connect this sprinkling to regeneration and baptismal symbolism. Lutheran teaching would likewise see water and Word joined in baptismal regeneration, though specific Lutheran page content on this verse was not fetched.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/regeneration (seen in excerpt)

**Spurgeon:** "From all your actual filthiness, as well as from all your original filthiness, will I cleanse you. From all your secret filthiness, and from all your public filthiness … 'From all your filthiness will I cleanse you.'"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/ (citing Spurgeon)

---

### vv. 26–27 — "A new heart … a new spirit … My Spirit within you"

**Traditional reading:** This is the most famous passage in the chapter — the promise of inward spiritual transformation under the new covenant. Three elements are distinguished:

1. **The new heart and new spirit (v. 26):** This is regeneration — the replacement of the "heart of stone" (dead, inflexible, unresponsive) with a "heart of flesh" (living, sensitive, responsive to God). The Expositor's Bible says: "The stony heart of the old nation, whose obduracy had dismayed so many prophets … shall be taken away, and instead of it they shall receive a heart of flesh, sensitive to spiritual influences and responsive to the divine will."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

2. **The indwelling Spirit (v. 27):** God promises to put His own Spirit within them. The Expositor's Bible comments: "The law, both moral and ceremonial, is the expression of Jehovah's holy nature, and both the will and the power to keep it perfectly must proceed from the indwelling of His Holy Spirit in the people."

3. **Enabled obedience:** "Cause you to walk in My statutes" — the Spirit empowers obedience from the inside out, rather than law being imposed from outside.

Ellicott notes this echoes Ezekiel 11:18–20 and Jeremiah 31:31–34.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

**Connection to the New Testament:** Jesus referred to this when speaking of being "born again" in John 3. Paul spoke of believers as "new creations" (2 Cor 5:17) and of the indwelling Spirit (Rom 8:9).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

---

#### TRADITIONAL DIFFERENCES ON vv. 26–27

**Reformed / Calvinist view:** This passage is a premier proof-text for the doctrine that **regeneration precedes faith**. Ligonier (R. C. Sproul) states: "The biblical doctrine of salvation can be summed up effectively in three words: regeneration precedes faith. Without regeneration, we cannot trust Christ." God sovereignly gives the new heart; only then can a person respond in faith and obedience. The "heart of stone" is incapable of responding to the gospel — God must act first.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/new-heart-flesh
— https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/regeneration

Michael Barrett (Monergism): "The old heart is a stone. It is lifeless, hard, and unfeeling. This is a vivid image of the helplessness and hopelessness of the human heart that is dead in sin… You would wait forever before you could find a spark of life in a stone, but here is the grace of the gospel: the Lord takes away the lifeless heart and gives a new one."
— https://www.monergism.com/efficacious-grace-%E2%80%93-ezekiel-3622%E2%80%9332 (from search excerpt)

**Wesleyan / Methodist / Arminian view:** While specific Wesleyan sources on this chapter were not fetched, the traditional Wesleyan reading would emphasize that God's promise of a new heart and Spirit is offered to all, but requires human cooperation — the "new heart" is given in response to faith, not prior to it. Ezekiel 18:31 ("make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit") is often cited as the human side of the same reality. God's grace is prevenient (goes before), enabling the sinner to respond, but does not irresistibly cause regeneration apart from faith.

**Pentecostal / Charismatic view:** Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal-influenced) reads vv. 26–27 as new covenant promises that apply to all believers now through Christ. The indwelling Spirit (v. 27) is linked to the baptism of the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:5, 8). The "cause you to walk" speaks of the Spirit-empowered life of obedience.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-36/

**Lutheran view:** Lutherans would connect the "sprinkling of clean water" (v. 25) with baptismal regeneration and the gift of the Spirit. The new heart is given through the means of grace — Word and Sacrament. God works through these external means to create inward faith and renewal. (Specific Lutheran page on this chapter was not available for detailed notes.)

**Dispensational / Literalist view:** Precept Austin (citing MacArthur) insists this chapter "must be understood to speak of a literal Israel, a literal land, and a literal regeneration, leading to a literal kingdom under Messiah." The promise of the new heart and Spirit is for ethnic Israel and will be fulfilled nationally at Christ's return. While individual Jews and Gentiles now experience this through the New Covenant in Christ, the national fulfillment awaits the millennium. MacArthur: "This chapter presents the prerequisite regeneration which Israel must experience before they can nationally enter into the promised blessings."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_36_commentary

---

### v. 28 — "You will live in the land … you will be My people, and I will be your God"

**Traditional reading:** This is the classic covenant formula (cf. Lev 26:12; Jer 31:33). The land promise is tied inseparably to the spiritual relationship. Ellicott notes that "the Israelites were not yet able to seek the spiritual, except as connected with the temporal blessing; and, indeed, the temporal was, in the ordering of Providence, a necessary means to the spiritual. Therefore the promise of earthly restoration must yet be made, and must in due time be literally fulfilled."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

---

### vv. 29–30 — "I will save you from all your uncleanness … summon the grain … no famine"

**Traditional reading:** The cleansing promised here is ongoing — not just from past idolatries but from "that ordinary sinfulness of man which, being continually renewed, needs continual forgiveness" (Ellicott). Alongside spiritual salvation, God promises agricultural abundance: plentiful grain, fruitful trees, abundant crops — reversing the "reproach of famine" that had marked Israel among the nations (cf. Ezek 34:29).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

---

### vv. 31–32 — "You will remember your evil ways … loathe yourselves … Be ashamed"

**Traditional reading:** The effect of God's goodness is genuine repentance. The Expositor's Bible explains: "Remembering what their past history has been, and contrasting it with the blessedness they now enjoy, they shall be filled with shame and self-contempt, loathing themselves for their iniquities … It is not meant that all feelings of joy and gratitude will be swallowed up in the consciousness of unworthiness; but this is the feeling that will be called forth by the memory of their past transgressions." God repeats (v. 32): "It is not for your sake that I will act." This is the "deepest compunction and self-abasement" that grace produces — the best moral guarantee against relapse.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

---

### vv. 33–36 — "The desolate land will become like the garden of Eden"

**Traditional reading:** The cleansing of the people and the rebuilding of cities go together. The transformation is so dramatic that passers-by will compare it to the Garden of Eden (cf. Gen 13:10; Isa 51:3; Joel 2:3). Ellicott suggests this points beyond mere agricultural prosperity to "that state in which man shall again be entirely freed from sin, which has been the state for which the Church in all ages has been preparing."

The Expositor's Bible: "To the heathen … the state of Israel will be a convincing demonstration of the power and godhead of Jehovah. Men will say, 'Yonder land, which was desolate, has become like the garden of Eden.'" The surrounding nations will know that Yahweh has done it.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

---

### v. 37 — "Once again I will hear the plea of the house of Israel"

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott notes the contrast with Ezekiel 14:3–4 and 20:3, where God formerly refused to be inquired of by a people whose hearts were far from Him. Now that He has given them a new heart, "He is ready to hear them." Prayer is restored as part of the renewed relationship.

The Expositor's Bible describes this as God promising to multiply the people "like a flock" — a response to the mood of dejection when the population was reduced. "In those days men will be as numerous as the sheep that flock into Jerusalem for sacrifice at the sacred festivals."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-36.html

---

### v. 38 — "Like the numerous flocks for sacrifices at Jerusalem … the ruined cities will be filled with flocks of people"

**Traditional reading:** The comparison is to the vast numbers of sacrificial animals brought to Jerusalem at the great annual feasts (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles). The image conveys not just numerical abundance but also consecration — "these flocks were devoted to the Lord" (Ellicott). The chapter ends with the recognition formula: "Then they will know that I am the LORD."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-36.html

---

## Summary of Major Points of Traditional Difference

| Issue | View |
|---|---|
| **Fulfillment timing** | **Dispensational/literalist** (MacArthur, Walvoord, Precept Austin): Full literal fulfillment awaits future millennium. **Covenant/amillennial** (Ellicott, Expositor's Bible): Earthly promises were types of spiritual blessings; some were fulfilled historically; ultimate fulfillment is in Christ and the Church. |
| **Regeneration and faith (vv. 26–27)** | **Reformed** (Ligonier/Sproul, Monergism/Barrett): Regeneration precedes faith; God sovereignly gives the new heart. **Arminian/Wesleyan**: God's grace enables faith; regeneration follows human response (Ezek 18:31). |
| **Sprinkling clean water (v. 25)** | **Lutheran/Anglican/Catholic**: Seen as pointing to baptismal regeneration. **Baptist/Evangelical**: Symbolic of spiritual cleansing by the Word and Spirit, not necessarily tied to the sacrament of baptism. |
| **"For My holy name's sake" (vv. 22–23, 32)** | All traditions affirm that God acts for His own glory. **Reformed** emphasizes this as proof of unconditional election. **Other traditions** see it as God's commitment to His redemptive purposes despite human failure, without necessarily implying unconditional individual election. |
